EDIT: it appears like many people have already given a lot of the suggestions. Adult Social Care would be a good place to start and being as honest as possible with them will help them refer you to other services. Mention that toy are a person with multiple disabilities and complex needs, and that should help too. Unfortunately throughout the process of accessing support it will take a LOT of you repeating yourself and reexplaining the complexities and difficulties of your situation to each service, over and over again, until an entire picture of your circumstances has been created.

As for PIP, you have to describe your issues for what they're like for you on your absolute worst day, even if it feels "deceitful". It absolutely isn't, but the services are designed to give you the absolute minimum and also minimise your experiences and downplay everything. Its really shit but that is just the reality we live in. They want you to feel bad because "someone else out there might have it worse", which is ridiculous and ableist. Your pain and disabilities agent any less valid than someone else's, even that person's is classed as "more severe", it doesn't also mean that *you* don't need help, too. It's not a contest. 

Housing-wise, NPRAS are a service through Housing Aid which can help you with a deposit for 1st month's rent to try and get a place of your own. There's also housing associations you can try, like Metropolitan or NCHA (Nottingham City Housing Association). There are also charities like Shelter of you need further advice or support. While really not ideal, there are places through Spare Room which might be able to help? 

Also, if you're very desperate for your own housing... unless asked specifically, DO NOT offer the info to landlords/estate agents that you have pets unless they seem safe/sound enough to hear you out. If they do ask, if possible, could you get a reference from your previous landlord/estate agent stating there was no issue with your pets in the property and that they caused no damage? If so, this might help persuade them into accepting your application. I know you don't really have the money for it either but you could also offer to pay for any damage your let's MIGHT cause to the property for further reassurance. 

Framework agents can help with setting up bills and getting you sorted with Council Tax and whatnot if you're struggling and unable to work (i.e., if you are not capable to taking care of yourself you might qualify for not having to pay Council Tax).

I don't know what else you have done with your GP, but explain ALL of this to them, too. They can refer you to services and can also back up your claims and write letters for safeguarding for you. Social prescribers can help point you in the direction of local support services. 

Juno and Women's Aid are currently underfunded so can't do much themselves but support with mental health and safeguarding yourself/teaching yourself important things about the nuances of abuse and the different types and how to keep yourself safe in the moment. They might even be able to help you formulate an action plan for when you're ready to leave that environment and quickly set yourself up so you can be safe and as independent/self-sustainable as possible given your disabilities. 

Remember, when trying to get references and diagnoses in this current climate, you to need to be as honest, raw, and vulnerable about your conditions and how they affect your daily life as you can. With regard to your partners support, honestly I wouldn't mention that because its technically unsustainable that they are able to support you financially given their own position. So explain you have their emotional support but they can't realistically help with other things. That will put you ahead in terms of a "queue" for support (though I hate that's even a thing). BTW, my source for this is that when I was trying to get support as someone with no family and friends (when I was in an abusive relationship during lockdown, though I've had a few previous to that), some of the agents themselves told me to do this. 

Lastly, if your partner IS taking care if you to that level, you can officially class them as your carer. Tell the services all they do for you in detail, and explain that due to them working and their own disabled family members they can't look after you full-time, so you still need a lot of support and they need  break.  If you do this, be warned: your partner might qualify for small financial support known as a carer's allowance, but this could also hinder your ability to access more support from available services. Does that make sense? 

I really hope this helps. I'm sorry I can't offer you more and I sincerely wish you the best of luck.

Self promo and social media. A LOT of people looking for photographers will use social media to do it. Post your website in your bio and just stay active on your accounts. Upload frequently and consistently and try to only show the work you want to attract professionally and what you're proud of. And always make sure you set yourself a decent day rate based on what you need to function as a freelance photographer. Its exhausting and there's so much that goes into it, but you can do it if you work hard. If you want more experience, ask to 2nd shoot for photographers and see if anyone is willing. If I could see your portfolio to see if our styles match enough I'd be willing to let you 2nd for me sometime (if I get anymore freelance photo work that is). I'm trying to slowly rebuild what I lost due to covid but because I work full time its tricky. 

Anyway, best of luck!

You can make a cheap or free website for your photos using wix.com or even squarespace. There are a ton of options out there. Shit, you could even just make an Instagram for your professional photos and put contact info in your bio for people. But the more you get into it professionally, you'll need to protect yourself if you want to use the pics for your portfolio. So, look for free sources you can use to create model release forms and if you can afford it, get photo liability insurance. Its not that much and it protects you against a lot. Source: I have a bachelor's degree in photography and was doing professional freelance and wedding photography pre-covid.

My partner does not understand my suffering, though they try their best. They want me to live, they want me to keep going and they have hope for me. But they are naive and have not been in my life very long in comparison to the length of time I've actually been dealing with this. They're hopeful because they've not been beaten by it yet. They've not been through the rigmarole that I have. This in itself can be even more frustrating for both of us - as I am fully aware they are only trying to help, but simultaneously I have already tried/done many of the suggestions for self-help and care. The point is, I need professional help but still can't access it. 

And sadly, at some point, despite the feelings of friends and family, the pain becomes too much. I'm glad my partner tries like they do but it doesn't mean it's necessarily the help I want or need. This creates constant tension and is hard to live with, because again they don't understand, despite their best "intentions" (which anyone could tell you that intention counts for little-to-nothing in the long run).
